SMTO-FIL-0001 — Permission error while handling the request

GUID: 9b74ac5b-4a10-4d58-8ebb-9d83bb2a9e16
Slug: permission-error
Domain: FIL · Subsystem: files

What happened

  • The computer refused to let SMTO open or change a file or folder it needed. The account SMTO runs as isn't allowed to use that item.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Open Technical details in this panel and look for the name of the file or folder that was refused. Knowing the exact item tells you whose permissions need checking.
  2. If you chose that file or folder, pick one in your own folders instead, or ask SMTO to save to a folder you can change. SMTO can only use places its account on that computer may read or write.
  3. If you need that exact item, ask the person who manages that computer to give SMTO's account access to just that file or folder. Allowing one item fixes this without opening up the rest of the computer.

What success looks like

  • SMTO reads or saves the item without a permission message.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't make whole folders or drives open to everyone just to get past this.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • A PermissionError (EACCES/EPERM) was raised, or legacy text matching "permission denied" was found, while accessing a filesystem resource the request needed.

What this means

  • Resolution received PermissionError, or the legacy unstructured fallback recognized permission-denied text after structured identity lookup failed. File and transfer receipts retain per-item execution, publication, cleanup and partial-effect facts. These explanations do not modify files, weaken path guards or replay a write; reconcile the original state before further mutation.

Why this can happen

  • Resolution received PermissionError, or the legacy unstructured fallback recognized permission-denied text after structured identity lookup failed.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the original structured operation and safe OS facts before changing permissions; a legacy text match alone is limited evidence.

How to fix it

  • Find the denied path in the technical detail or the Server/Gateway log (the OS message usually names it), then check owner, mode and ACLs for the account running the Server or Gateway (ls -l and getfacl, or icacls on Windows). Grant only the needed access to that path, or use an authorized destination instead.
  • Check OS/filesystem permissions for the referenced resource, or use an authorized identity or destination.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • The intended identity can access the exact authorized resource without broadening unrelated permissions.

What not to do

  • Do not repeatedly submit the same invalid input; correct the named constraint first.

Technical notes

  • File and transfer receipts retain per-item execution, publication, cleanup and partial-effect facts. These explanations do not modify files, weaken path guards or replay a write; reconcile the original state before further mutation.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
